articles.title: BYD Carmais amplia estrutura em Parnamirim com alta dos eletrificados | G1
articles.standfirst: Nova unidade fortalece atendimento e pós-venda para clientes da marca na Grande Natal
articles.summary: Nova unidade fortalece atendimento e pós-venda para clientes da marca na Grande Natal
articles.body:
Nova estrutura da BYD Carmais em Parnamirim amplia atendimento e pós-venda no RN. — Foto: Divulgação

O crescimento dos veículos elétricos e híbridos no Rio Grande do Norte tem redesenhado o mercado automotivo e ampliado a necessidade de uma rede preparada para atender esse novo perfil de consumidor. Mais do que acompanhar o aumento nas vendas, o setor passa a demandar investimentos em assistência, manutenção especializada e suporte no pós-venda.

Inserida nesse cenário, a BYD Carmais está na reta final da implantação de sua nova unidade em Nova Parnamirim, às margens da BR-101. O espaço, com cerca de 8 mil metros quadrados, foi concebido para reforçar a presença da marca na região e ampliar a capacidade de atendimento aos clientes da Grande Natal.

A nova concessionária reunirá showroom, oficina com estrutura ampliada, equipe técnica especializada e estoque de peças, em uma operação pensada para oferecer mais eficiência no atendimento e maior agilidade nos serviços. A proposta é atender de forma ainda mais completa os proprietários de veículos da marca em Parnamirim, Natal e municípios vizinhos.

Unidade em Nova Parnamirim foi planejada para acompanhar crescimento da frota eletrificada. — Foto: Divulgação

Com o avanço da frota de eletrificados no estado, cresce também a exigência por estruturas adequadas para manutenção e assistência. Nesse contexto, a expansão da BYD Carmais busca responder a uma demanda que vai além da comercialização de veículos, acompanhando toda a jornada do cliente após a compra.

“Nosso compromisso é crescer junto com o mercado, investindo não apenas em vendas, mas principalmente na experiência do cliente após a compra. A nova unidade chega para ampliar ainda mais a nossa capacidade de atendimento, com uma estrutura robusta de pós-venda, oficina e estoque de peças, preparada para acompanhar o crescimento da nossa base de clientes na região” , destaca Leonardo Dall'Olio, diretor comercial do Grupo Carmais.

A nova estrutura também reflete a consolidação da mobilidade elétrica como uma tendência cada vez mais presente no mercado potiguar. À medida que esse segmento avança, torna-se essencial contar com profissionais capacitados, equipamentos específicos e uma operação apta a atender as particularidades dos veículos eletrificados.

Expansão da BYD Carmais acompanha nova fase da mobilidade elétrica no RN. — Foto: Divulgação

Para Eduardo Weimar, diretor comercial da BYD Carmais, esse movimento precisa ser acompanhado por uma expansão que considere todas as etapas da experiência do consumidor com a marca.

“O crescimento da frota de veículos eletrificados traz também uma responsabilidade maior com quem já escolheu a marca. Por isso, estamos investindo em uma estrutura que vai muito além do showroom. Teremos uma oficina ampla, equipe especializada e um estoque de peças preparado para atender uma demanda cada vez maior. Queremos que o cliente perceba esse investimento também no pós-venda e na qualidade do atendimento” , afirma.

Em fase final de preparação, a nova BYD Carmais Parnamirim marca um novo passo da empresa na Região Metropolitana de Natal e reforça um movimento cada vez mais estratégico no setor: crescer em estrutura, atendimento e relacionamento na mesma velocidade em que avança a mobilidade elétrica.

articles.title: Pak takes SCO chair, PM Modi slams use of terror as strategic asset
articles.summary: India News: Framing security as a non-negotiable prerequisite for regional progress, PM Narendra Modi delivered a thinly veiled warning to Pakistan over state-spo.
articles.body: Framing security as a non-negotiable prerequisite for regional progress, PM Narendra Modi delivered a thinly veiled warning to Pakistan over state-sponsored terrorism at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit. With Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif in attendance, Modi said countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy, and provide shelter and support to terrorists, must be sent a strong message that terrorism can never be a strategic asset for anyone.The remarks are significant also because of the timing. Pakistan assumed rotating chairmanship of SCO from Kyrgyzstan on Tuesday and will host the heads-of-state summit next year, for which it will invite Modi, along with others.Modi made the remarks, in which he also warned against double standards on terrorism, while expanding on India's SCO vision - Security, Connectivity and Opportunity - that he articulated in Tianjin last year.With Chinese President Xi Jinping also present, PM reiterated India's position that all connectivity initiatives must respect sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states as this is also the "fundamental spirit" of SCO charter. Modi said that terrorism continued to pose a serious challenge to humanity and it's important to not remain confined to an action-reaction approach in the fight against the menace.“We must dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorist financing, recruitment, radicalisation, and safe havens. We must speak with one voice and make it clear that there can be no place for double standards on this serious issue,” said PM, without naming Pakistan as SCO charter doesn’t allow members to raise bilateral differences.India and Pakistan together joined the China-dominated Eurasian grouping as full members in 2017. For India, the security-oriented SCO has served as a platform not just to assert its strategic autonomy but also flag regional risks from state-sponsored terrorism. Modi said that the bloc’s shared aspiration for a peaceful and secure Eurasia is also closely linked to peace and stability in Afghanistan and that India will continue to contribute to the development and provision of humanitarian assistance to people of the country.Modi addressed West Asia crisis, saying it was affecting energy security, maritime trade and supply chains around the world and recalling his message earlier that conflicts cannot be resolved on the battlefield. “Countries of Global South bear greatest brunt of such disruptions. Therefore, India has consistently called for all tensions and conflicts to be resolved not on battlefield, but through dialogue and diplomacy,” he added.While underlining the importance India attaches to SCO, Modi said that at a time when the world is passing through instability, the organisation must transform the shared geography into opportunities and bring about positive change in people’s lives. Describing SCO as a confluence of great civilisations, cultures, and ideas, he said that over next 25 years, people-to-people ties should remain at the heart of cooperation among the member states.“True measure of our success should be how many new opportunities our efforts create, how many new markets open up for entrepreneurs, how much farmers benefit from tech, and how much better the lives of our citizens become,” said the PM. According to an Indian readout of PM’s participation, Modi stated that strong and trusted connectivity initiatives were important for the group’s shared progress and prosperity.“Underlining that India supports connectivity efforts that link markets, enhance trade and open new opportunities for development, he reiterated such efforts should respect sovereignty and territorial integrity of nations,” said the readout.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Zelensky warns airlines Russia’s sky ‘completely unsafe’
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines on Tuesday against flying into Russian airspace as his military responds to an “escalation” in missile and drone attacks. Zelensky said in an evening address that Russia has recently changed its defense tactics, focusing on strikes from Ukrainian airspace. After the most recent wave of attacks, the Ukrainian president…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines on Tuesday against flying into Russian airspace as his military responds to an “escalation” in missile and drone attacks.

Zelensky said in an evening address that Russia has recently changed its defense tactics, focusing on strikes from Ukrainian airspace. After the most recent wave of attacks, the Ukrainian president added, this type of warfare “cannot and will not remain confined” to his country’s territory.

“Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” he continued .

Zelensky directed the warning at countries with embassies in Ukraine and Russia, as well as at airlines flying to airports in Moscow, St. Petersburg and “other key [Russian] destinations.” However, he clarified the country’s threats do not apply to civilian aircrafts.

The Ukrainian president also noted his Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other agencies will provide “full information” to international entities on the impending “dangers” in Russian airspace.

During his address, Zelensky confirmed a Russian ballistic missile struck Kyiv on Monday accompanied by “numerous drone strikes” on other Ukrainian cities.

On Tuesday, the Ukrainian president said Russia struck a railway depot where there “was no military equipment whatsoever.”

Ukraine has ramped up its production of long-range weapons during the four-plus-year war , boosting its arsenals of drones and cruise missiles with assistance from foreign partners.

“Two years ago, Russia’s advantage was this huge country that we couldn’t reach into,” Oleg Krot, the founder of Ukrainian weapons Culver Aerospace, recently told The Wall Street Journal .

Krot added that Ukraine’s weapons are now “only at the beginning of the real capabilities they will have over the next few years.”

Russian strikes killed 437 Ukrainian civilians in July, marking the deadliest month for civilians in the eastern European nation since May 2022, according to the United Nations’ (UN) Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine .

July also saw the highest number of child Ukraine War casualties since April 2022, with 17 Ukrainian children killed and another 166 injured, per the UN.

“Civilian casualties from aerial bombardments (105 killed; 753 injured) increased by 143 per cent compared with June 2026 (45 killed; 308 injured), with glide bombs becoming the second leading cause of civilian casualties,” the UN mission noted in its Aug. 12 report.

German officials on Tuesday also accused Russia of being behind a drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.

“Although the Russian authorities are not properly informing people about this, Russian airspace will effectively be closing — the war started by Russia is closing its skies,” Zelensky said Tuesday. “We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost.

He added, “That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over.”

articles.title: PM Modi repeats call to 'shun unnecessary gold buys, foreign weddings & holidays'
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Buoyed by the better-than-expected GDP growth, PM Modi on Tuesday lauded Indian economy's resilience during a period of global crises. He a.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Buoyed by the better-than-expected GDP growth, PM Modi on Tuesday lauded Indian economy's resilience during a period of global crises. He again pushed for swadeshi goods and urged citizens to shun overseas weddings, foreign vacations and avoid unnecessary gold purchases at a time when imports remain elevated due to high commodity prices in the wake of the West Asia conflict.His appeal against buying gold also puts to rest speculation around import duties being reviewed by govt. In fact, Centre and RBI are keeping a close watch on shipments. Since Jan, both quantity of gold and value of imports have increased. Since Modi's first appeal in May, however, there has been a drop in quantity of imports but the value of imports is rising due to higher prices, albeit at a slower pace. At $3.5 a kg, the unit value of gold was 94% higher in June, but prices have moderated to $2.8 a kg, which was 47% more than a year ago.Since Modi’s first appeal in May, gold import quantity has dropped, but import value is rising due to higher prices, albeit slower. Prices moderated to $2.8 a kg, 47% more than a year ago.While gold remains an investment option for households, higher prices have deterred consumers from buying large quantities, with recycling of old jewellery also rising, industry executives said.Modi also mounted a withering attack on LoP Rahul Gandhi for spreading pessimism about growth, dismissing his criticism as “jhooth ki goonj”. This was Modi’s second reaction to the growth rate within 24 hours. His message mixed praise for people’s hard work with disdain for critics like Rahul and reiterated his call to citizens to avoid non-essential gold purchases and foreign trips.“We have to maintain this pace and keep growing and, for this, aatmanirbhar Bharat is essential,” he said in a selfie-video posted on Instagram.GDP grew at 7.8% in the April-June quarter, bringing relief to the NDA govt, which has been buffeted by the opposition parties, especially Congress under Rahul, over alleged misgovernance. Modi said, “There are people within India who are mired in despair, ‘jhooth ki goonj’, and are busy spreading pessimism everywhere.”Emphasising India’s feat, Modi said it came amid global conflicts and crises, causing supply-chain disruption. Since Covid in 2020, stability has remained elusive for the world but India is progressing at a fast pace, he added.Opposition has a right to criticise govt but especially Congress shouldn’t insult people by being incorrigible naysayers and call India a dead economy when data speaks otherwise, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said.BJP played up Rahul’s dismissive comments about the economy to contrast them with India’s growth. Besides his dead economy jibe, Rahul claimed a crisis unseen in people’s lifetime would hit the economy. An economic tsunami was coming, he had said. Modi said his govt’s policy is right and intentions clear, calling upon people to work hard. India’s collective strength will take it to new heights. By emphasising swadeshi and self-reliance, people will bequeath a developed India to the young generation.At a press conference, BJP’s Ravi Shankar Prakash demanded Rahul apologise. As leader of opposition, Rahul’s comments carry weight, he said. The world has begun taking them lightly as he makes misleading remarks, while Pakistan plays them up.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1985, a Florida couple moved into a 1908 house and spent 41 years preserving it; it has now become Manatee County’s first local historic landmark
articles.summary: US News: The walls of this Florida house have witnessed more than a century of history, including 41 years with the same couple who refused to let its past dis.
articles.body: The walls of this Florida house have witnessed more than a century of history, including 41 years with the same couple who refused to let its past disappear. After moving into the 1908 home in 1985, Margi and Pat Nanney devoted decades to preserving its original character. The home has now become Manatee County's first local historic landmark. The three-story Johnson Helm House in Oneco, Florida, has retained much of the character it had when it was built in 1908. Original features including its woodwork, windows, floors and staircase have survived, offering a glimpse into the area's past. The home was already recognised on the National Register of Historic Places, but its latest distinction is different. The Manatee County Commission unanimously approved the property as the county's first locally designated historic landmark, according to Bay News 9.A 1908 Florida homeThe Johnson Helm House dates back to the early 20th century and is associated with Johnson and Fannie Helm, who were among the property's early residents. The house is notable not simply because of its age. According to WWSB, it was designed in the Richardsonian Romanesque Revival style, an architectural style characterised by substantial forms, arched openings and elaborate masonry. The style is uncommon along Florida's Suncoast, adding to the home's architectural importance. Inside, many original details remain. The house still has its original floors, windows, woodwork and staircase. The staircase includes hand-carved newel posts, while historic photographs preserved by the Nanneys offer a visual record of how the property looked more than a century ago. The home has remained remarkably intact despite the changes that have taken place around it.A family's 41-year connectionThe Nanneys moved into the house in 1985, beginning what would become more than four decades of caring for the property. Rather than extensively modernising the historic structure, they worked to retain its original features. According to Bay News 9, Nanney said the house is still approximately 95% original. The property also became the setting for the Nanneys' own family history. Their children were born in 1988 and 1992, and height marks made on the walls remain as reminders of their childhood.Over the years, the couple also collected photographs and other materials connected to the home's history. Some descendants of the original owners eventually reached out to the Nanneys, helping add further pieces to the story of the house. For Margi Nanney, maintaining an old property has been a long-term commitment rather than a simple renovation project. The years of work have helped ensure that details from the home's early history were not lost.First local landmarkThe new designation gives the Johnson Helm House a distinction it did not previously have. Although the property was already listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the county's local designation provides another level of recognition and protection. Bay News 9 reported that Manatee County Commissioner Amanda Ballard said the County established its local historic designation process about 13 years ago, but the Johnson Helm House is the first property to complete the process and receive the designation. The county's approval also means future changes to the property will be subject to review. That helps protect the historic characteristics that made the house eligible for the designation in the first place. The approval followed about a year of work on the designation process. The Manatee County Commission ultimately voted unanimously to recognise the property.Preserving Oneco's pastThe significance of the Johnson Helm House extends beyond the building itself. The property is located in Oneco, a community whose history is closely connected with agriculture, citrus growing and nurseries. The Nanneys hope the recognition of their home can help draw greater attention to that history.Their preservation efforts also show how historic buildings can remain part of everyday life rather than becoming simply preserved objects. For 41 years, the Johnson Helm House has been both a family home and a link to an earlier period of Manatee County. The Nanneys have even considered a future in which the house could become more accessible to the public.A house with more history aheadMore than a century after it was built, the Johnson Helm House has now entered another chapter. The home survived changes in its surroundings, remained largely intact and spent 41 years in the care of one family. Its original architectural details continue to tell the story of the people who lived there and the community that grew around it. Now, as Manatee County's first local historic landmark, the 1908 house has gained an official place in the county's preserved history. For the Nanneys, that recognition represents more than an honour. It is a way of ensuring that the work they began when they moved in during 1985 can continue long after their own 41-year chapter with the house has ended.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Remarkable US oil deal puzzles analysts - and angers many Venezuelans
articles.summary: Amounting to 65 billion barrels of crude, the deal is labelled by one ex-envoy as a colonialist "fever dream".
articles.body:
From the moment elite US troops swooped into Nicolás Maduro's compound in Caracas to forcibly remove him from power in January, President Donald Trump made clear that securing control over Venezuela's oil resources was a key goal of his administration.

The United States would "run" Venezuela, he said at the time, and manage the sale of Venezuelan oil for the foreseeable future.

The signing of a huge US-Venezuela oil deal in Caracas on Wednesday marked the fruition of that plan. The agreement grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela, amounting to a staggering 65 billion barrels of crude. That equates to more than a fifth of the country's proven oil reserves.

Beyond the eye-watering numbers, both sides heralded the deal as good for their respective nations.

President Trump called it "the biggest oil deal in world history", while the interim Venezuelan President, Delcy Rodríguez, said the agreement was "historic", and would generate $100bn (£74bn) in investment and more than $200bn in tax revenue.

"This is a terrible deal. [Rodríguez] has given away 20% of the national patrimony for nothing," said Trump's former special representative on Venezuela and Iran, Elliott Abrams. "I think she is simply complying with the demands she's getting from Washington."

On Tuesday, the White House released a fact sheet which set out some details of the deal's framework. The US government will work alongside a private business in Venezuela called North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep), the second largest private oil producer in Venezuela after Chevron.

One extraordinary detail of how the Trump administration will work with Nabep is that the US government will have "veto power over the appointment of any member of the board of directors, and a majority of Nabep's board of directors must be US citizens".

With the ongoing US war with Iran increasing prices at the petrol pumps, a boost in oil production outside of the Middle East could affect consumers.

Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum told Fox Business the pact was "shifting the geopolitical centre of the global energy markets" away from what he called the "choke points in the Middle East" and back to the Western Hemisphere.

There is a logic to the US-Venezuela partnership, Elliott Abrams argued, while Gulf oil supplies are currently so unreliable. But he said the terms are so one-sided they are a "kind of fever dream of what colonialism looks like".

The White House has spoken of the deal having "re-established the Monroe Doctrine", an 18th Century principle exerting US power across South America - "purging foreign malign influence from our backyard and ensuring American dominance in our hemisphere is never again questioned".

Despite the insistence from both governments that the plan will benefit both Venezuelans and Americans, it is not without pitfalls and clear unanswered questions.

The proposed timeframe alone is problematic. Trump has said the agreement will generate profit within two or three years. Energy experts, however, warn the dire state of the Venezuelan oil sector means a decade is more realistic.

Luis Pacheco, of the Baker Institute at Rice University in Houston, told BBC Mundo that Venezuela needs to invest about $100bn over eight years in order to return to its oil production levels of 30 years ago.

"It's important to know who will manage those resources and for what purpose," Pacheco said.

"Are they going to put the same people in charge of managing that money who already squandered the biggest oil boom of the century?" he asked, referring to past mismanagement of the country's oil wealth.

The Venezuelan opposition is concerned the deal deepens President Trump's relationship with Delcy Rodríguez, whom they accuse of heading the same regime as Maduro.

The Trump administration not only decried Maduro's government as a corrupt drug cartel, but surrounded Venezuela with the biggest armada of the modern era.

The ease and speed with which Washington has now pivoted to working with Maduro's former vice-president infuriates the opposition.

The Nobel Peace Prize winner and presidential hopeful, María Corina Machado, may choose not to publicly criticise President Trump, whose support she needs if she hopes to come to power. Others, though, have been more forthcoming.

"You chose to use the power of the United States not to liberate Venezuelans, but to ally yourself with our oppressors," said Venezuelan economist, Ricardo Hausmann, on social media, directing his comments at the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"You opted to push through an asset seizure, an unconstitutional agreement with an illegitimate and oppressive government, instead of using the leadership of the United States to first restore constitutional order and democracy," he said.

The lack of an imminent election in Venezuela – or, indeed, any clear plan towards one – strikes many opponents as a betrayal.

There is betrayal felt at the other end of the ideological spectrum, too. Although the governing socialist party, PSUV, has backed Rodríguez over the US deal, many Venezuelan socialists see it as capitulation.

After almost three decades opposing Washington's influence in the region, they feel she has gifted the country's most valuable asset to the old enemy.

The deal "hands over [the oil] and opens the doors to a new colonialism of the United States," said Rafael Ramírez, who served as the head of the state-run energy firm, PDVSA, and as the oil minister under former President Hugo Chávez.

In early 2008, Chávez presented his Sunday television programme, Aló Presidente, from former ExxonMobil oilfields in the Orinoco River Belt.

Having expropriated some of the oil company's assets in the region, he was in a defiant mood.

"We have the reins in our hands and we won't ever let them go again," he said of the state-run oil company's ownership of oilfields, and denounced how previous Washington-friendly governments had turned Venezuela into "a nation of gringos".

"It was a theft of our nation but the Bolivarian Revolution has put a stop to it," he thundered to applause from PDVSA employees.

Yet it was one of his disciples – his handpicked successor's successor – who has now signed this opaque deal with Washington and praised it as a victory for Venezuela.

articles.title: IAEA calls for access to Iran nuclear sites over proliferation concerns
articles.summary: IAEA says lack of information and access to facilities to verify Iran’s nuclear material is a proliferation concern.
articles.body:
The International Atomic Energy Agency ( IAEA ) has called for “utmost urgency” to address the lack of access to Iran’s nuclear sites .

In a quarterly report seen by news agencies on Tuesday, the United Nations nuclear watchdog labelled its “lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of proliferation concern”.

The US has claimed preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon – an ambition that Tehran continues to deny – as the motivation for the war that it launched in March. However, Tehran has been successful in shifting the focus of the hostilities to control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway.

In particular, the IAEA report raised concerns over the lack of access to the Isfahan plant, which was targeted several times by the US and Israel over the past year or so.

In the report, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi expressed his “conviction that the long-standing problems and recurrent crises surrounding these issues must be resolved through a long-lasting, verifiable diplomatic agreement”.

However, Iran has said that access to the sites that have been struck by military action must be arranged via special arrangement.

The head of Iran’s Atomic Energy Organization, Mohammad Eslami, said on August 26 that the IAEA “cannot seek to inspect these centres until it develops specific criteria and protocols for inspecting sites targeted by military attacks”.

Tehran suspended cooperation with the UN nuclear watchdog following US and Israeli attacks on Iran in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites before saying in September 2025 it would allow the UN agency’s inspectors to return.

However, access to the nuclear sites that have been bombed has not yet been granted. Despite US President Donald Trump having claimed last year that the US had destroyed the facilities and crippled Tehran’s nuclear programme, Iran’s stores of enriched uranium remain unaccounted for.

Tehran has repeatedly denied any military ambition linked to its nuclear programme, insisting on its right to the technology for civilian purposes.

However, the IAEA, whose latest report will be discussed at its board of governors meeting from September 21-25, has reported in the past that the level of Iran’s enrichment of its uranium reserves is well above that needed for civilian purposes, although neither is it at the level of weapons grade.

images.caption: International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi speaks during a news conference at United Nations headquarters [File: Jason DeCrow/AP]

articles.title: Actress Eve Arden left Hollywood’s smog for a California farm, joining a forgotten era when stars owned working land outside Los Angeles
articles.summary: US News: In June 1971, actress Eve Arden and her husband, actor Brooks West, were living a life that placed them far from the image of Hollywood most people as.
articles.body: In June 1971, actress Eve Arden and her husband, actor Brooks West, were living a life that placed them far from the image of Hollywood most people associated with them. In a United Press International column written by Hollywood correspondent Vernon Scott and published in the Perry Daily Journal on June 21, Scott noted that the couple owned farmland about an hour's drive from downtown Hollywood and lived on the ranch because they preferred it to inhaling Los Angeles smog. They were part of a wider group of film and television stars who owned ranches and farmland across California and the American West, sometimes as investments and sometimes as places to eventually retire. Scott's column highlighted celebrities including Bob Hope, Bing Crosby, Jimmy Stewart, Randolph Scott, Robert Stack, Jim Nabors, Buddy Ebsen, Jim Arness, Joel McCrea and Ronald Reagan, showing how land ownership had become a notable part of the financial and personal lives of Hollywood figures by the early 1970s.Why Hollywood stars were buying ranches and farmland across the WestScott opened his column by describing motion picture and television stars among the ranch and farmland owners of the West, saying they bought real estate either as investments or as places to retire. Bob Hope was identified as one of the largest individual landholders in Southern California, with thousands of acres of expensive real estate. His friend Bing Crosby was described as owning ranches in Northern California as well as parcels around the San Francisco area, while Jimmy Stewart had a cattle ranch about two hours from Los Angeles. Randolph Scott, who had long been absent from the screen, had accumulated substantial wealth through real estate negotiations. In the San Luis Obispo area, Scott listed extensive holdings belonging to Frank Sinatra, Lucille Ball, Fred Astaire and Robert Mitchum, noting that Mitchum operated a horse ranch on his property. The column also pointed out that not every celebrity intended to actively use the land. Some stars, Scott wrote, purchased anywhere from 100 acres to tens of thousands of acres and allowed the properties to lie fallow before eventually selling them as prices increased.Why Jim Nabors, Buddy Ebsen and Jim Arness treated their properties differentlyThe land owned by the stars varied considerably in how it was used. Jim Nabors, best known at the time for television, owned what Scott called an immense farm in the fertile Coachella Valley south of Palm Springs. Unlike acreage being held simply for future appreciation, Nabors' property was producing what Scott described as bountiful cash crops. Buddy Ebsen was another television star who had converted his earnings into real estate, while Jim Arness of Gunsmoke owned more than 1,000 acres of what Scott called prime ranch country in the mountains beyond the San Fernando Valley. Arness' father handled the horses and cattle on the property. Robert Stack, meanwhile, owned acreage in the Sacramento area that included a game preserve and duck club. These examples show that there was no single model for celebrity land ownership. Some stars treated their acreage as an investment, others used it for farming or ranching, and still others turned their properties into recreational retreats. Eve Arden and Brooks West represented another variation: they actually lived on their farmland, choosing the quieter setting outside Hollywood over the city's air.How Joel McCrea and Ronald Reagan turned land into long-term wealthScott particularly singled out Joel McCrea as one of the earliest actors to recognize the financial potential of Southern California real estate. According to the column, McCrea's dealings in land had come to dwarf his considerable earnings from acting over the years. Ronald Reagan, who had not yet become California's governor when the column appeared, was also building a substantial property portfolio. Scott wrote that Reagan had bought hundreds of acres in Los Angeles County and had since purchased another 771 acres in Riverside County, where he planned to retire. The column also offered a glimpse into how some of these transactions were structured. Scott wrote that many stars bought property through corporate names because it was less expensive that way. The appeal of land was partly its independence from the entertainment business: Scott's column observed that networks, agencies and sponsors could cancel a show or otherwise affect a career, but they could not cancel a parcel of ground. For actors whose careers depended on studios, television networks and changing audiences, land offered an asset that existed outside that system.What Eve Arden's ranch reveals about Hollywood in 1971Eve Arden's appearance in Scott's column is brief, but it captures one of the more personal reasons celebrities were acquiring property away from Los Angeles. Arden and West owned farmland only about an hour from downtown Hollywood and actually chose to live there, according to Scott, because they preferred it to the city's smog. Their decision was part of a broader pattern the column documented across the West, where actors and television stars were buying everything from working farms and cattle ranches to game preserves and undeveloped acreage. More than five decades later, the article offers a contemporary snapshot of Hollywood wealth at a time when the entertainment industry and Southern California's expanding real estate market were becoming increasingly intertwined. The stars Scott named were not all using their properties in the same way, but their purchases reflected a common attraction to land as something that could provide income, recreation, a future retirement home or simply an escape from Los Angeles. For Arden, the appeal appears to have been especially straightforward: a place to live where the air was preferable to Hollywood's.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: '1 tick, 2 ticks': Kin seek hope in text-delivery reports in Nepal
articles.summary: South Asia News: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT, NEPAL): For two days after Serbian citizen Enisa Lekovic disappeared in the floods in Nepal, a WhatsApp message sent by her .
articles.body: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT, NEPAL): For two days after Serbian citizen Enisa Lekovic disappeared in the floods in Nepal, a WhatsApp message sent by her daughter sat on a single grey tick - sent, but not delivered. Then, on Aug 28, the screen changed: the tick had turned into two blue ones - the family's first real sign of hope. On Tuesday, that hope turned into relief when her daughter, Ines Todorovic, confirmed that Lekovic had been found alive and was on her way to Kathmandu. "I can't describe what I felt these days," she wrote on social media.Like Lekovic's family, relatives of hydropower workers missing in the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli flood began turning phones into search evidence after rescue teams could not provide definite answers. They repeatedly sent messages, watching whether single grey ticks turned into two, while many bypassed conventional search desks and approached Nepal Police Cyber Bureau, Nepal Telecom, Ncell and rescue teams with mobile numbers, asking them to trace the last tower and sector where the phones had been active before signals disappeared.For families with little else to go on, a change in message-delivery status or a last tower ping became a potential clue to where a missing relative might be - and where rescuers should look next.Relatives of Roshan Kumar Joshi, an environmental expert from Morang working at the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project, repeatedly messaged him after he went out of contact. "Roshan, are you safe? Please reply as soon as you find any connectivity," read one. The single tick did not change as relatives searched social media, contacted project staff and waited for news. At the Upper Trishuli-3B Hydropower Project, relatives of engineer Pramila Pathak, 32, wrote: "Pramila, are rescue teams near your quarters? Send a location pin if your phone turns on." That message too remained undelivered.Telecom officials, however, said that a single grey tick could not show whether someone was alive, trapped or even carrying a functioning phone. Nepal Telecom said that after power supplies failed in affected areas, it shut down data and other services and kept only 2G voice services running to conserve battery backup. Internet-based messaging platforms such as WhatsApp could not deliver messages.Private mobile operator Ncell also issued a statement cautioning against drawing conclusions from a phone going offline. "A phone can disappear from the network because it was damaged by water or because its battery ran out. Disconnection does not necessarily mean the person was caught in the disaster. They may have reached safety and simply run out of battery."Meanwhile, the last mobile tower and sector used by a handset offered a more specific geographical clue. Families approached the Nepal Police Cyber Bureau, Nepal Telecom, Ncell and rescue teams with mobile numbers and requests to establish where missing workers' phones had last connected before signals disappeared. Joshi's family eventually received one such record: "Ramche-C, 9.10am, Aug 26." It showed that his handset had last connected through sector C of the Ramche tower in Rasuwa, allowing relatives to narrow the direction in which they wanted rescuers to search. Chitragupta Bhatta, who worked at Trishuli Hydropower Company Limited, left another significant digital trace. His family received: "Neupane Chaur, 9.26am, Aug 26." His phone remained active more than 15 minutes after the flood struck the area, raising hopes that he might have reached or remained inside a tunnel. "...We began to hope that perhaps he is inside a tunnel," a relative said. "So many days have passed... It is becoming difficult to hold on."A senior executive with Huawei Nepal said mobile towers generally divided coverage into three directional sectors. "By mapping the direction, we can determine whether the phone was on the river side or the mountain side."Privacy rules created another hurdle. Families could move beyond physical search desks in their hunt for clues, but telecom operators could not directly hand them subscriber's location records. A Nepal Telecom said such information is shared with security agencies through authorised channels.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Springfield, Ohio, Haitian student dies by suicide after ICE mandates ankle monitor following TPS loss
articles.summary: Pierre Damas Bel, 20, expressed feeling “shame and humiliation” at having to wear by an ankle monitor. The college student died by suicide days later.
articles.body: Hours before Ohio college student and athlete Pierre Damas Bel took his own life Monday morning, he called his father for help. It was around 8 a.m., and he was sitting inside his car on the side of Interstate 70, struggling mentally and emotionally with the shame of being forced to wear an ankle monitor by immigration officials. Bel, a 20-year-old Haitian student at Wright State University, said he had been bullied at school and felt “humiliated” by the device. “I told him to come home so we can talk,” Bel’s father said in an emailed statement. “Around 11 the police showed at my door to report that my son threw himself under a truck.” Bel stepped into oncoming traffic and died from his injuries, the Ohio State Highway Patrol said. His family blamed the humiliation brought on by the ankle monitor he had been wearing since July. Carl Ruby, a local pastor and immigration advocate, said in a statement that Bel’s family wanted people to know it was a suicide related to immigration policies. Bel arrived in the U.S. in 2024 and applied for admission into the country using the now-defunct CBP One app, Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in an emailed statement. He was released into the country and settled in Springfield with his parents and two brothers. Bel excelled in academics and athletics, becoming an honor roll student at Springfield High School and joining JROTC. He was recruited to play soccer at Wittenberg University and hoped to attend medical school after college, immigration advocates said. In May, the Springfield City School District featured Bel in a Facebook post highlighting recipients of a local scholarship that offered $2,500 to each student. Bel wore a blue suit and a black bow tie as he accepted his award, with a big smile on his face. The future seemed bright. Things began to change July 29, when ICE placed him in an “alternatives to detention program” with an ankle monitor while he continued his immigration proceedings. He documented the experience on social media, writing July 30 that he came to the country to study, not “commit a crime or hurt anyone.” “Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience,” he wrote. Bel was one of the roughly 300,000 Haitian nationals living in the U.S. who lost their temporary protected status, or TPS, at the end of July following a Supreme Court decision. The policy change triggered a wave of fear and confusion in Springfield, where 12,000 Haitians live. ICE said it does not comment on the cause of death while an investigation is pending. “We will not speculate about unverified claims regarding other individuals,” it said in an emailed statement. According to the Wittenberg University men’s soccer team, Bel was no longer able to play for the team after he lost TPS. He transferred to nearby Wright State University and immediately faced taunts and bullying from students, his family said. “We do not want to politicize this, but this is a political problem, and the only solution is a political solution,” Ruby told reporters Tuesday. “The only way that this will never be correct is if Republican elected officials join us in demanding better policy,” he said. Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, has criticized the Trump administration’s harsh immigration enforcement and its impact on Ohio residents. On Tuesday, he called Bel’s suicide a “horrible tragedy” that never should have happened. “I think we have to ask ourselves: Is this really good? Is it what we want done to people like this being picked up and facing deportation? Do we want that being done in our name?” he told reporters. Springfield, a small city in southwestern Ohio, became the center of salacious and unfounded rumors about the Haitian community during the 2024 presidential election. In August, ICE began alerting Haitians to appear in person at check-ins, where they were given ankle monitors to track their whereabouts until immigration judges can decide whether they may have legitimate reasons to remain in the country, such as asylum claims. Ankle monitors are usually issued because of a lack of detention space for more than 300,000 Haitians who lost TPS after the Supreme Court decision in June, a senior Department of Homeland Security official has said. Some Springfield residents saw the arrival of Haitian nationals as a driving force behind the city’s economic renaissance. Others complained that Springfield was not prepared to welcome so many immigrants, who contributed to long waits at clinics and were driving up rental prices. Despite the unwanted attention, many Haitian residents thrived in their adopted home, taking jobs in manufacturing, buying homes and opening businesses. Occasionally tensions boiled over. White supremacist groups and alt-right influencers have clashed with local immigration advocates and faith leaders who sought to protect the Haitian community. Viles Dorsainvil, co-founder and executive director of the Haitian Support Center, said the Bel family is one of several hundred who have poured into the center seeking legal help and guidance. He estimates 34 people have been detained since TPS ended. Bel’s is believed to be the first suicide in Springfield related to immigration enforcement, he said. “I know many folks are depressed right now,” Dorsainvil said. “I never had in my mind that it would have gotten to that point.” If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

images.caption: A photo shared by Wittenberg University of Pierre Damas Bel, a freshman soccer recruit who died after stepping into traffic in Springfield, Ohio on Aug. 31, 2026.

articles.title: Ariana Grande completes tour and steps back from public life
articles.summary: The star makes an emotional farewell as she wraps up a tour she's described as her "last hurrah".
articles.body:
Ariana Grande made an emotional exit on Tuesday night, as she wrapped up her Eternal Sunshine tour, and prepared to step back from public life.

The singer was occasionally close to tears - most notably during One Last Time, the song that took on extra meaning as an anthem for survivors of the 2017 Manchester terror attack.

"London, I'm going to need you to help me on this one," she said, kneeling down to be near the audience throughout the performance.

Last month, Grande announced a break from all future public-facing appearances following months of intense speculation about her health and appearance.

The step-back includes Grande's withdrawal from a production of Stephen Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George at London's Barbican next summer.

She was due to appear alongside her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey. He also pulled out of the production on Tuesday.

On stage in London, Grande showed no signs of fragility or poor health - other than a foot injury that required her to swap her trademark stilettos for a succession of knee-high platform boots.

Nonetheless, she sprang across the stage in sync with her dancers, often on tip-toe to compensate for the lost height of her high heels.

But her voice faltered again during the song Nowhere, Nobody, as she sang the line: "Hard to believe in a perfect ending."

The blip was short-lived, though. Professional to the core, Grande regained her composure and was never less than magnetic on stage.

Addressing the audience towards the end of the show, the singer thanked fans for their support.

"This has been one of the most beautiful extraordinary experiences of my life and I just wanted to express my gratitude without sobbing completely," she said.

"I'll cherish this experience always. I have the best fans in the entire world and I always have. Thank you for all of your effort and continuing to make this so special.

"I have loved every minute of this with you all and I just wanted to make sure I express how grateful I am."

Grande announced her hiatus last month, shortly after releasing the music video for her latest single, Petal, which led some fans to express concern about her weight.

One wrote on X that the 33-year-old had "become so thin that people are genuinely concerned".

Two days later, Grande's publicist announced her "step back from visibility" , due to "endless, ongoing public scrutiny".

Speaking to People magazine, a source close to the singer noted that she "performs a very physical show... healthily and successfully at a very high level night after night".

Grande herself moved to reassure fans the following night, saying her decision came from a "thoughtful, empowered place" , and had been planned "a long time ago".

"I heard my fans were worried negativity was ruining things for me but... that could not be more than the opposite," she said on stage in Chicago.

"Boundaries need to be set, human beings do need a break sometimes."

Even before that announcement, Grande had described the Eternal Sunshine tour - which started in the US in June - as "one last hurrah", saying she wanted to take more acting roles after her Oscar-nominated performance in Wicked.

That meant her 10 show residency at London's O2 Arena represented many fans' last chance to see her in concert.

They flew in from all over the world - from China and Australia and cities all across Europe - with 200,000 people attending the London dates alone.

On the second night, Grande surprised the audience by bringing out her Wicked co-star Cynthia Erivo for a rendition of their movie duet For Good.

Across the board, reviews were positive.

"There's no question about it - Ariana Grande is one of the best singers of her generation," wrote Rolling Stone magazine , noting that "there were no signs" of the singer "struggling or not wanting to be there".

The Telegraph called the show "flawless" , praising its "Hollywood-indebted" staging, and Grande's "genuine affection for Britain".

The BBC's review highlighted quieter songs like Imperfect For You , describing them as "delicate and gorgeous and strangely intimate in a room of 20,000 people".

But Guardian writer Kate Solomon said she was "gripped by genuine concern" for Grande, even when she was enjoying the show, adding: "I really hope this tour does not go down in history for the wrong reasons".

The NME, by contrast, was left breathless by the star's physical prowess.

"Throughout the show," marvelled Nick Levine , "she skips across the stage in skyscraper heels that most drag performers would baulk at."

That wasn't the case on the final night, however, due to what Grande described as a "deep cut" on her foot.

Writing on Instagram, she assured fans the injury wasn't serious, insisting she was "on the mend" and would complete her final shows "even if I am a few inches shorter than usual".

She did so with a huge smile spread across her face, leaning into the big notes of Dangerous Woman, and sprinting across the stage during Break Free - one of many up-tempo highlights.

She ended the show as she always does - attached to a harness, ascending into the rafters of the O2 and disappearing.

Fans were left wondering when, if ever, they'd see her perform again.

Among them was Rachid, a London fan who said he was "devastated" by Grande's withdrawal from touring.

"That's why I really, really wanted to come to the last show because I was like, 'What if she never comes back?'" he said.

"So that's why I was here - to enjoy everything she has to give us, and hopefully she gets a nice break now."

"I'm not gonna lie, I'd do the same thing," joked Manchester fan Nadine.

"Like, I made my money, got on stage, sang my heart out... I'd bugger off, too! Straight to Hawaii, or somewhere else where nobody knows who I am, you know what I mean?"

Lukas, who’d travelled from France for the concert said it was good to see Grande taking matters into her own hands.

"She's said goodbye and now she's gonna rest for her safety," he said. "If she needs the break, she takes it and we, the real fans, understand."

"It's sad that people are speculating about someone else's health," said Polish fan Alejandro Grande (no relation, he insisted).

"And it's sad that she has to make a decision for herself just to reclaim her power and her energy."

"Yeah, it's completely up to her," agreed Bella Hopkins from Bronsgrove. "I think people should respect how she feels and what she needs."

articles.title: 2015 quake drove Haku families to flood-hit Trishuli banks
articles.summary: South Asia News: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NEPAL): Hundreds of Tamang families uprooted from Haku and adjoining mountain villages in Nepal's Rasuwa district by the 2015 Gorkha .
articles.body: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NEPAL): Hundreds of Tamang families uprooted from Haku and adjoining mountain villages in Nepal's Rasuwa district by the 2015 Gorkha earthquake were still living in settlements along the Trishuli river 11 years later when the Aug 26 flood swept through Khalte, Pairebesi, Mailung and adjoining areas.Around 100 children are sheltering at the Shivalaya Basic School in Uttargaya after the disaster, with 60 students left without both parents.Prakash Nepal, a teacher at Shri Nilkantha Secondary School, linked the toll to the post-quake displacement. "The displaced settlements were relocated along the riverbank," he told TOI. "That is why there was such a heavy human toll this time." The school had around 550 students; nearly 200 remain out of contact, while four staff are also missing. Three other schools were also destroyed.Khalte was among the worst-hit. It had 257 houses before the flood and not one remained intact, said Purna Bahadur Ghale, 43, an executive member of Uttargaya Rural Municipality whose family had been displaced in 2015. "I must have gone to Singha Durbar more than a hundred times to ask govt to move us somewhere safer," he said. "They always said they would, but they never did." Seven of his relatives were missing.The chain of displacement began after the 7.8-magnitude earthquake on April 25, 2015, triggered landslides and rockfalls across Haku, Gogane, Tiru and Mailung. The authorities moved hundreds of families into shelters downhill. A final assessment released in June 2017 identified 113 households for relocation and found Gogane, Tiru and Mailung unsuitable for habitation. But the place where many families subsequently settled - Khalte on Trishuli's bank - was itself later assessed as unsafe. By 2019, a total of 269 displaced families were living there.Attempts to move them permanently repeatedly stalled. The danger along the river was already evident. On July 8, 2025, rapid discharge from a supraglacial lake on Purepu Glacier in Tibet sent a flash flood down the Lende-Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridor, killing at least nine people and leaving 19 missing. Weeks later, after Khalte was hit by another flood, resident Lalmaya Tamang, 29, warned: "The river can take everything at any time."A year later, many of the same families were displaced once again.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The compounding climate hazards creating prime flood conditions
articles.summary: Wildfires, heavy rains and other factors on a warming Earth are contributing to intense flash flooding, including the Grand Canyon.
articles.body: Welcome to the daily Inside Scoop newsletter. We’ve been hearing harrowing stories from survivors of Saturday’s deadly flash flooding in the Grand Canyon, which was likely part of a chain of extreme weather events. Also, an NBC News crew was attacked while reporting in the West Bank. Let’s get into it. A massive wildfire that tore through parts of Grand Canyon National Park in July 2025 likely helped set the stage for the treacherous flash floods that killed two hikers over the weekend. Dozens were rescued and at least one person is still missing.

articles.title: Best hikes to try around Lubbock ahead of Texas Tech's week one matchup with Abilene Christian
articles.summary: Lubbock Lake Landmark, Buffalo Springs Lake, and Caprock Canyons State Park top the list of must-hike trails near the Texas Tech game this weekend.
articles.body: With week zero of the college football season in the books, we turn our attention to the main course: week one. Dozens of college football games will be played this weekend in a ton of amazing cities across the country, and many of you will be making your way out to these venues to take in some of the action. Much like with week zero, we here at OutKick OutDoors wanted to give you some of the best hiking spots in some of the most unique and picturesque destinations, and this weekend on the docket is Lubbock, Texas. FIVE BEST HIKES IN TALLAHASSEE TO TRY AHEAD OF FLORIDA STATE AND NEW MEXICO STATE'S WEEK ZERO SHOWDOWN The 12th-ranked Texas Tech Red Raiders will be taking on the Abilene Christian Wildcats, and if you are making the trip to see this game in person, chances are you are going to want to explore all the natural beauty that the area has to offer. Much like with our week zero hiking spots highlight for Tallahassee, this one comes with a heat warning. HIKING ETIQUETTE RULES THAT SHOULD BE COMMON SENSE BUT APPARENTLY NEED TO BE SPELLED OUT FOR SOME PEOPLE West Texas in September is an oven, and it's a dry heat at that. You won't sweat quite as much as you might in the Florida Panhandle, but that just means the dehydration will sneak up on you, so make sure you're staying hydrated and dress appropriately. With all that said, let's unpack everything Lubbock has to offer. Lubbock Lake Landmark Consider this one the "must do" for anyone not from the Lubbock area. Lubbock Lake Landmark offers quintessential West Texas views and wide open spaces for a relatively easy hike. The entire trail includes nearly five miles of hiking and sits right along the Yellowhouse Draw, combining mixed-grass prairies with an archeological dig site. If you're into history, the trail takes you right past the excavation site and gives hikers a view of thousands of years of human occupation. And if the combination of West Texas views and archeological history doesn't sell you on Lubbock Lake Landmark, here's the real kicker: admission is free! You can't beat that price point. Dunbar Historical Lake If you're looking for less of a "touristy" destination, Dunbar Historical Lake is the pick. The East Loop of the trail offers a two-mile hike that is a solid workout for beginning hikers, while the West Loop offers a more hilly, five-mile experience that will put your glutes and quads to the test. The actual elevation changes and dirt trails all winding around a lake will challenge you while also giving you some great views of the natural beauty that Lubbock has to offer. THESE ARE THE DEFINITIVE UNWRITTEN RULES OF CAMPGROUND ETIQUETTE EVERYONE SHOULD KNOW If you're a mountain biker, this site has some added appeal for you as well, as the trail is super popular among the biking community. Dunbar Historical Lake is super convenient to get to, sandwiched between several major thoroughfares, but it never feels too close to the urban sprawl. Buffalo Springs Lake I promise they won't all be lakes! For anyone looking for the best scenery that Lubbock has to offer without venturing too far outside the city limits, Buffalo Springs Lake offers outstanding canyon and lake views. The 1.7-mile nature trail built by the Llano Estacado Audubon Society is definitely something to write home about, as you start out on the bluffs before making your way down towards the shores of the lake. Bird watchers will also get an added bonus, as there are plenty of different aviary species that call this park home. One thing to note, the trails aren't super well-manicured nor are they regularly groomed, so this is an example of "roughing it" for a hike. With that said, the trails are well worth it, and with the added camping, fishing, and water activities provided here, Buffalo Springs Lake should absolutely be on your list. Mae Simmons Park Are you looking for wilderness vibes without straying from the city? Mae Simmons Park has you covered. You can get your fill of the Yellowhouse Canyon without ever having to leave the comfort of Lubbock at this local hidden gem. Both hikers and mountain bikers swear by Mae Simmons Park, and the trail network offers great views and wild terrain that ditches the conventional walking paths of most city hikes. Locals swear by this park, as hikers from the area give Mae Simmons Park high marks, and the Outer Loop Trail in particular is one worth checking out. Consider this an option if you don't want to burn an entire half a day driving to enjoy the great outdoors. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Caprock Canyons State Park This last one is a bit off the beaten path, but I promise it's worth it. For those of you making an extended stay in Lubbock, Caprock Canyons State Park is 90 miles outside the city limits, so make sure you dedicate a day for this one. With that said, the trail is simply astounding. Caprock Canyons offers 25 miles of trails, red-rock canyons, and challenging hikes for even the most seasoned veterans. If you happen to be one of those veteran hikers, might I suggest the Haynes Ridge Overlook, a 2.3-mile trail that is a serious workout and features a 600-foot ascent with some of the best views in the entire state. Wildlife lovers will have plenty to cheer about too, as the park boasts a large population of bison roaming throughout the area. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There are so many trails to pick from, it's almost like a "choose your own adventure" in hiking form, so load up the car and don't miss out on this stunner of a state park.

articles.title: CBS chief Bari Weiss' involvement in viral El-Sayed report sparks debate among critics
articles.summary: The involvement of CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss in a viral report about Dem hopeful Abdul El-Sayed's deleted 9/11 tweets sparks fierce debate.
articles.body: The alleged involvement of CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss in a report about Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has fueled a fiery debate on social media. The network drew far-left outrage Monday for a report putting a spotlight on El-Sayed's deleted posts about 9/11 and linking them to the forthcoming 25th anniversary of the terrorist attack. "As the nation prepares to mark 25 years since Sept. 11, 2001, Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, may be facing the risk of renewed scrutiny and fresh political attack," CBS News wrote Monday. CBS NEWS TAKES HEAT OVER REPORT ON DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED'S NOW-DELETED 9/11 POSTS Later that evening, Status News reported that Weiss "praised the story during the network's daily editorial meeting" and that she "personally directed that the headline be tweaked to specifically mention that El-Sayed had deleted tweets referencing the September 11 terrorist attacks." Weiss' version of the headline, which was published, "Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's deleted tweets on Sept. 11 attacks invite scrutiny of past remarks," provided context to the substance of the report. Fox News Digital learned the pre-Weiss headline originally read, "For Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, Sept. 11 commemoration invites scrutiny of past remarks." SOCIALIST CANDIDATES CAN DELETE OLD POSTS, BUT THEY CAN'T ERASE THEIR RADICALISM Many on the left viewed Weiss' involvement in the El-Sayed story as a "scandal." "A major scandal for CBS," the liberal outlet MeidasTouch reacted on X. "It should be a scandal that a major American news network is now led by an overt, hands-on, undisguised Islamophobe but... it isn't. Islamophobia has been normalized in our media, and in our country. Shamefully," Zeteo founder and former MSNBC host Mehdi Hasan wrote. "Not a good look whatsoever," Democratic strategist and podcast host Dan Turrentine said. "Democrats: CBS must not be invited/allowed to host any debate in which Dem candidate appears," former Washington Post columnist Jennifer Rubin declared on the liberal social media platform Bluesky. "The penalty for gutter racism and toadyism to a MAGA/fascist regime is that you do not get accorded treatment as a real news outlet. PERIOD." Meanwhile, many conservatives laughed off the zealous reactions from the left and the report's findings about Weiss doing her job. "So she’s the editor-in-chief?" National Review senior editor Charles C.W. Cooke reacted. "How dare she improve the objective journalism of the entity she is responsible for," The Federalist editor-in-chief and Fox News contributor Mollie Hemingway replied. "An editor does editing. News at 11," Washington Free Beacon reporter Chuck Ross quipped. "Fascinated by the Bari Derangement Syndrome," GOP strategist Matt Whitlock reacted. "The Democrat candidate in the top Senate race in the country has been deleting tweets about how he feels about 9/11... After campaigning with a surrogate who said America deserved 9/11. Seems pretty newsworthy!" CBS News did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The CBS report cited El-Sayed's deleted social media posts, including some from 2020 comparing the nearly 3,000 Americans killed on 9/11 to the death toll from the coronavirus pandemic. Another post from Sept. 11, 2021, first uncovered by The Washington Free Beacon, read, "Today, I mourn the 3K lives, 6K injuries, & infrastructural devastation in NYC, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my faith. Tomorrow, I'll mourn ~1M lives, millions of injuries, & infrastructural devastation in 3 countries, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my country." UNEARTHED EL-SAYED ESSAY DRAWS EXPLOSIVE TRUMP-BIN LADEN PARALLEL: ‘RECRUITED, RADICALIZED AND REASSURED’ El-Sayed was confronted about his deleted posts by a local CBS News reporter on the campaign trail. "What happened on 9/11 is a disaster. It was a terrible attack on our country," El-Sayed said. "And our responsibility is also to think about, how do we build an America where we are protecting our servicemen and women from being asked to fight in wars we have no business fighting in?" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A CBS News source familiar with the story previously shrugged off the criticism, telling Fox News Digital that reports about deleted social media posts from politicians are published "all the time."

articles.title: Van Jones calls out El-Sayed for ‘insane’ belief that he’s ‘smarter than Barack Obama’ on Israel policy
articles.summary: Van Jones called Abdul El-Sayed's total arms embargo stance against Israel "insane" and questioned whether he thinks he's smarter than Barack Obama.
articles.body: CNN host and former advisor to President Barack Obama Van Jones questioned if Michigan Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed thought he was "smarter than Barack Obama" on foreign policy in fiery comments discussing the "dangerous" beliefs held by many progressive figures in the Democratic Party. El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel and former CNN commentator, has been embroiled in political controversies regarding his stance toward Israel and his relationship with a famous left-wing livestreamer, Hasan Piker. In late August, Jones appeared on the "Ask Haviv Anything" podcast, where he addressed how the long and historic alliance between Black and Jewish Americans has recently fractured. He went on to criticize El-Sayed over his stance on Israel, saying, "his positions on Israel and foreign policy are insane." "Look, some Democrats are going to say that we should condition military aid. That, you know, 'Israel's gone too far in Gaza and in the West Bank and in Lebanon. We're going to put some conditions on you.' I think that's a defensible position if you're a Democrat," he said. "That's not Abdul's position." VAN JONES WARNS FAR-LEFT SOCIALIST AGENDA IS 'REGRESSIVE' THREAT TO DEMOCRATIC PARTY "I can get why you would say, ‘No more aid, they got to pay their own way.' That’s not Abdul’s position. Abdul’s position is a total and complete arms embargo against the state of Israel, including defensive weapons. That’s an insane position," Jones continued. "That says, if Israel wants to pay for interceptors to stop a rocket coming from Iran or coming from Hezbollah or coming from Hamas, an interceptor, we should deny them the right to buy the interceptors to knock down rockets going at Israeli children, women, men, babies. That’s an insane position." Jones went on to question if El-Sayed believed he was wiser than Obama on U.S. policy toward Israel. "And by the way, it offends me because that’s — you know, Barack Obama was a part of creating that Iron Dome. Barack Obama was a part of creating those interceptors. Barack Obama thought that the Israeli people were in such a tough neighborhood, they needed to be able to knock down rockets," Jones recalled. "So you’re telling me you’re smarter than Barack Obama? You have better ideas about foreign policy than Barack Obama? And you want to de-plug and defund and take away Israel’s — half the world’s Jews'— ability to defend themselves? That's an insane position." "The fact that people are having a hard time figuring out what to do about it, I find alarming," he continued. "This is not acceptable." MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE CONFRONTED REPEATEDLY OVER ISRAEL’S RIGHT TO EXIST, DEFUNDING THE POLICE Julian Epstein, a Democratic consultant and former chief counsel to the House Judiciary Committee, argued that El-Sayed has a long pattern of concerning positions and statements. "Bless Van Jones' heart, I agree with him," Epstein said in comments to Fox News Digital. "To my mind, El Sayed is clearly aligned with the Muslim Brotherhood propaganda machine that gives a pass to the butchering of millions of Arabs by extremist Islamist overlords in the Middle East while slandering Israel with lies like a 'apartheid' and 'genocide' to justify the exterminationist and racist ideology that has always driven this conflict." Theo Wold, former assistant attorney general and former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy under President Donald Trump warned that El-Sayed is part of a generational phenomenon of migrant populations taking up radical positions as they gain political power. "Abdul El-Sayed is not a one-off. He’s the avatar of the rising generation of Third World immigrants who were resettled in the United States over the last thirty years," Wold said. "Visit a high school classroom in Anaheim or Queens, and you’re likely to encounter similar radical claptrap. El-Sayed’s foreign policy is more ‘global south’ than it is American. His messaging is so radically foreign to American ears because it’s just that: radical and foreign. And increasingly, that’s what the post-American, pro-Antifa Democrat Party has become, as well." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Jesse Arm, a Manhattan Institute vice president and pollster who was born in Michigan, said that Van Jones deserved credit "for drawing a clear and principled line" on the issue, arguing that Black Democrats are being sidelined by the radical wing of their party. "Jones’s frustration reflects a larger struggle within the Democratic Party. Reasonable liberals like him — especially those rooted in the African American community —recognize that they are losing control of a party they helped build. As the Democratic coalition becomes Whiter, richer, and more ideologically extreme, the preferences of most Black voters are increasingly subordinated to those of the party’s new activist base," he added further. "Fringe extremists like El-Sayed and his top campaign surrogate, the racist streamer Hasan Piker, are seeking to marginalize and silence those voters, replacing the politics of the Black church with the politics of the campus encampment. There's a reason El-Sayed got crushed with African Americans in Michigan's Democratic primary, losing three-quarters of the Black vote to his more mainstream opponent." Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign about Van Jones' statements and did not receive an immediate reply.

articles.title: Soft launches to late sittings: Six ways to get cheaper meals out
articles.summary: The cost of dining out is getting increasingly hard to swallow - but clever planning can net you cheaper deals.
articles.body:
The price of eating out can be hard to swallow while the cost of living remains high, with more than a third of Brits cutting back on going to restaurants, according to YouGov's latest Dining Out report.

Restaurateurs say the rising cost of food, energy, wage and tax bills mean they've had to put up prices, with some top chefs campaigning for government help.

Many eateries are offering incentives to get diners through the doors. Here are some ways to save money on meals out.

Many restaurants offer points, freebies, discounts and birthday treats to keep customers coming back.

One of the most well-known is the Pizza Express Club. Regular diners can progress through a bronze, silver and gold system unlocking perks from free dough balls to hot and soft drinks on the house.

Nando's uses a chilli system for its loyalty programme, while other schemes such as Tastecard offer discounts at hundreds of eat-in and takeaway venues in exchange for an annual fee.

Restaurants often want to fill seats outside of peak lunch and dinner hours so opting for earlier or later sittings can be rewarded by a cheaper bill.

Apps such as First Table, which operates across 21 UK cities, as well as Ireland, New Zealand and Australia, give diners 50% off food when they book a participating restaurant's first or last dining slot. In exchange, diners pay a small booking fee.

EatClub is another, giving walk-ins up to 50% off the whole bill at thousands of venues when they redeem an offer within its app. The biggest discounts are at off-peak times.

Shokofeh Hejazi, director of foresight and innovation at global trends agency The Food People, says earlier dining appeals because it tends to be quieter and calmer, people drink less and it allows them to get home sooner.

Meeting up for breakfast also tends to be a bit more wallet-friendly as it's usually just one course and diners get the same catch-up time with friends and family, she adds.

In the school holidays, many places will entice families through their doors by offering free or £1 meals for kids eating with paying adults.

These range from big chains such as TGI Fridays, cafes at supermarkets including Morrisons and Asda, and even garden centres like Dobbies.

While some tie-in with school holidays, other deals are all year round.

Many new restaurants will offer discounts in a bid to encourage diners to try them out and spread the word that they've opened for business.

These are known as "soft launches" and can run for several weeks. They're a cost-effective way of trying a higher-end restaurant without such a hit to the wallet.

Keep track by signing up to newsletters that list upcoming openings in the local area.

Hejazi says some restaurants are extending the period before they fully open to garner more buzz, while others are making their soft launch pricing permanent for quieter days such as Mondays.

People shouldn't assume they're priced out of fine dining-type venues because "there's access points for everybody in a lot of these places", she says.

5. Make your supermarket points work harder

Supermarket loyalty points from those weekly shops add up over time so why not put them toward a meal out?

For example, each 50p earned in Tesco Clubcard points can be exchanged £1.50 in vouchers to spend at participating Prezzo Italian venues. The chain is just one of Tesco's restaurant partners.

Finally, there are plenty of options to take away food for free or at a fraction of the usual price.

Surplus food apps such as Too Good To Go, or Olio, allow customers to bag goodies that would otherwise go to waste.

It's a bit of a gamble - you don't always know precisely what you'll be getting.

But there's money to be saved on items needed to buy anyway, that's more cash left over for when you do decide to dine out.
