articles.title: A first-generation Florida rancher spent years saving to buy 660 acres; he is now protecting it for panthers and snakes
articles.summary: US News: A 660-acre working ranch in Florida’s Peace River Valley will now remain protected for generations, preserving a landscape where agriculture, water an.
articles.body: A 660-acre working ranch in Florida’s Peace River Valley will now remain protected for generations, preserving a landscape where agriculture, water and wildlife exist side by side. The Ludwig property in Hardee County sits along Brushy Creek, west of the Peace River, and contains grasslands, hardwood forests, wetlands and other important natural areas. Its owner, Keith Ludwig, spent years saving to purchase the land before placing it under a conservation easement. A first-generation rancher and lifelong oceanographic engineer, Ludwig can continue operating his cow-calf business while ensuring the property remains protected from future development. According to the Florida Conservation Group, the conservation effort will also help close an important gap in the Florida Wildlife Corridor, benefiting species including the Florida panther, indigo snake and Florida burrowing owl.How a first-generation Florida rancher saved for years to protect his 660-acre ranchFor Ludwig, owning a ranch was the result of years of planning and saving. Unlike someone born into a long-established ranching family, he became a rancher through his own efforts. The Florida Conservation Group described him as a first-generation rancher who had also spent his career as an oceanographic engineer. Yet his connection with agriculture had developed much earlier. Having grown up on a small farm in Indiana, Ludwig had long appreciated the work and commitment required to run a farm or ranch. When he eventually entered the cattle business, he learned directly from experienced local ranchers. They helped teach him how to manage cows and calves and showed him how a ranch could operate efficiently while respecting the land around it.Buying the 660-acre property gave Ludwig the opportunity to run his own cow-calf operation. However, ownership also presented him with another possibility of protecting the landscape permanently rather than leaving its future uncertain. The conservation easement on the property was made possible through the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services’ ‘Rural and Family Lands Protection Program.’ Through this arrangement, the ranch can continue operating while the land's important natural features remain protected.Importance of this Ludwig ranch for Florida’s wildlifeThe Ludwig property is more than a working cattle ranch. Its position in the Peace River Valley makes it part of a wider network of natural habitats. The surrounding landscape provides habitat for wildlife including the Florida panther, indigo snake and Florida burrowing owl. For Ludwig, this connection between ranching and wildlife conservation is one of the most meaningful aspects of protecting the property. The land can remain productive for agriculture without losing the natural areas that support Florida's native species. This is particularly important in a changing landscape where development can divide large natural areas into smaller and more isolated pieces. Protecting connected stretches of land gives wildlife more room to move through the wider landscape. Ludwig said he wanted to contribute to protecting Florida's distinctive natural environment and the resources that future generations will depend upon. His decision shows how private landowners can play a major role in conservation while continuing their everyday agricultural work.How does the 660-acre ranch help protect Florida’s waterThe importance of the Ludwig property also extends well beyond its boundaries. The ranch lies within the Brushy Creek basin and forms part of the larger Peace River Watershed. Across the property, surface waters move through mixed-wetland hardwood forests, marshes, grasslands and mesic flatwoods. These waterways eventually connect the ranch to the Peace River, Charlotte Harbor and, ultimately, the Gulf. The Florida Conservation Group says conserving the land can help improve water quality, support the replenishment of underground water supplies and reduce regional flooding.The wider Peace River Valley has particular importance for southwest Florida because the region supplies drinking water to nearly one million residents. Its waterways are also closely linked to the health of the Charlotte Harbor Estuary. For Ludwig, the knowledge that his ranch can help protect water resources far beyond his own property is a significant part of the conservation decision. The benefits of keeping the land intact can therefore reach downstream communities as well as the wildlife living closer to home. Charlotte Harbor is also an important recreational fishing area and a major part of southwest Florida's economy. Protecting the waterways that feed into it means protecting a larger system that supports both people and nature.One Florida rancher inspiring wider conservation effortsLudwig hopes that his decision will encourage other landowners in the region to consider conservation programmes. He believes the Rural and Family Lands Protection Program offers a way to protect wildlife and water while allowing ranchers to continue their operations. In his view, this makes conservation compatible with the long-term future of Florida's agricultural lands. The Florida Conservation Group has been working across the Peace River watershed to protect land surrounding important tributaries. Over the previous year, the organisation supported conservation easements covering 11,000 acres within the watershed.The Ludwig property adds another protected piece to that larger effort. Its 660 acres may be one ranch, but its impact reaches through connected wildlife habitat and waterways. Ludwig can continue raising cattle on the property while knowing that its forests, wetlands and grasslands will remain part of Florida's landscape. In the Peace River Valley, Ludwig's journey from aspiring rancher to landowner has ultimately become a story about leaving something behind that is bigger than the ranch itself.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Every rescue now a miracle’: 4,462 still missing in Nepal, hopes dim
articles.summary: South Asia News: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWANKOT, NEPAL): Death toll from the Aug 26 Himalayan flood rose to 1,066 across Nepal and Tibet on Tuesday, while 4,462 people rema.
articles.body: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWANKOT, NEPAL): Death toll from the Aug 26 Himalayan flood rose to 1,066 across Nepal and Tibet on Tuesday, while 4,462 people remained missing as rescue operations entered a critical phase.Of those killed, 1,050 were in Nepal and 16 in Tibet. Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority listed 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreign nationals, while China’s latest count listed another 546 missing in Tibet.Seven days after the flood, hope of finding survivors in the open along the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor dimmed sharply. Senior police officers and disaster management officials told TOI that, outside tunnels, underground powerhouses and other protected structures, “each successful rescue would now be a miracle”. This, even as teams searched stretches buried under sludge, boulders, uprooted trees and wreckage. “The sheer volume and force of the flash flood left virtually no accessible pockets of shelter along the open riverbanks,” a senior Nepal Police officer coordinating ground operations said.After seven days under heavy debris and hardened silt, finding anyone alive out in the open has become extremely unlikely. But we are not calling off the search.”Officials involved in surface searches said the force of the flood had stripped away settlements and vegetation along parts of the river corridor and deposited deep layers of mud, rock and timber downstream, leaving few protected spaces where someone caught in the open could survive for a week.A senior Nepalese army officer involved in downstream search efforts added, “Our field units and canine squads are covering massive stretches of silt, but the ground reality is exceptionally grim. Anyone caught in the open bore the direct brunt of heavy boulders and torrents. Our remaining operational hope for living survivors is largely concentrated on the underground project sites where air pockets might exist.”For India, the latest MEA missing-person list remained at 275 Indian nationals and 128 PIOs. MEA didn’t revise the figure on Tuesday. It said 158 Indian nationals had been rescued by Monday night.The strongest remaining hopes now centre on Nepal’s devastated hydropower projects. NDRRMA listed 639 people associated with hydel projects as missing, while Independent Power Producers’ Association Nepal (IPPAN) put 894 people “out of contact” across 11 projects.Officials and industry representatives estimated that around 500 could have been inside tunnels when the flood struck, though rescuers had not established precisely how many were underground.Floodwater, boulders and thick slurry blocked passages and collapsed tunnel sections. At Upper Trishuli-1, rescuers pushed around 160m inside before finding the passage blocked. At Chilime, teams reached about 150m before encountering a steep section that was completely buried.At Upper Trishuli-3A, rescuers used excavators, compressors and rock breakers to create an opening, but a rush of water prevented entry and forced them to try another approach. Access work continued at Upper Trishuli-3B.Indian specialist teams worked with Nepal army at Chilime and Langtang, while Chinese tunnel experts joined operations at Upper Trishuli-3A. An Indian team had probed up to 185m inside the Langtang tunnel. India also sent forensic specialists, including DNA experts, to help identify bodies.At Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, a thermal drone sent inside one tunnel detected no sign of life in the section it surveyed. Drone operator Manish Maharjan said mud, water and debris had filled 80-90% of the height of parts of the tunnel. He described some passages as being packed with mud “like toothpaste in a tube”.Yet the tunnels and underground powerhouses still offered what the devastated riverbanks did not — the possibility of protected chambers and pockets of air. Nepal Tunnelling Association secretary Chhatra Bahadur Basnet said there was still hope of finding survivors underground but warned that limited oxygen, food and water made every passing hour critical.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the studio with Kasabian: 'We never thought we'd see success again'
articles.summary: The rock band invite us into the studio to talk about the unexpected "third act" of their career.
articles.body:
"A little bit of hunger is good for you," says Serge Pizzorno. "Keeps you going."

The Kasabian frontman is describing a typical day in his home recording studio.

Snacks and phones are banned, but he might screen a film in the background (typically something by David Lynch) while he tinkers with his vast array of synths and guitars.

"No distractions, four or five hours a day. I like to work fast.

It's a big change from Kasabian's early days, where he'd "live the French poet life", staying up for three days straight, seeking inspiration at the limits of human endurance.

"That can be great," he says. "It adds to the atmosphere of a record. But for the last three albums, I've pretty much led a structured life, and I'm really digging it."

Serge has welcomed the BBC into his studio to preview Kasabian's ninth album, Act III, 10 days before its release.

To get there, you drive deep into rural Leicestershire, to a gated house where you're greeted by his wife, Amy, and two gorgeous but "unruly" dogs.

A framed photo of Kasabian's recent Finsbury Park gig sits in bubble wrap at the foot of the stairs. Serge's own artworks, including a distorted Count Duckula and a vintage apothecary cabinet, decorate the kitchen.

He shuffles in from a side room, effortlessly cool in his dog-print designer shirt , and leads us outside. Stepping over a pile of discarded Nerf guns, we pass through a gate into a secret walled garden.

There sits the studio, an austere black cube jutting into the countryside, guarded by a giant sculpture of a gorilla.

As we enter, a pharmacist's sign lights up with the studio's nickname, "The Sergery" (a pun stretched to its limits in 2025 when Serge became an honorary doctor of music ).

In the corner, a gong sits in silence, waiting to be struck. And four bobblehead Kasabian dolls (rescued from the Call video ) nod in unison as Serge cues up the new music.

He plays us Soulmate, a funny and affectionate tribute to Amy, powered by a peacocking guitar riff. Then it's Say You (Closer), whose message of togetherness brims with gorgeous three-part harmonies.

It's the closest Kasabian have ever come to sounding like The Eagles; and the thought of recreating on stage live is giving the musician jitters.

In rehearsals, "there are moments where it does sound like the Eagles, and there are moments where it sounds like three pissed up people in a pub," he laughs.

"What I'm going to do, hopefully, is get the crowd to do that bit."

He may be joking, but the album's focus on Tunes You Can Sing™ is entirely deliberate.

"I feel like it's not a very melodic time in music," Serge says. "So I was personally yearning for hooks and verses that are as powerful as choruses. Like an Elton John song where the melody just breaks your heart."

He goes full Elton on the single Hippie Sunshine , whose lairy, chanted chorus is suddenly interrupted by a twinkling piano breakdown.

"I love those 60s songs like Good Vibrations and Baron Saturday, where the middle is just a handbrake turn, and you go, 'Where the hell am I now?'" says Serge.

"The first few times you hear it, you're like, 'Oh, that's weird'. Then you get used to it, and it becomes the exciting bit, the part everyone waits for."

But the musical contrasts in Hippie Sunshine serve a bigger purpose.

The verses are a critique of soulless tech oligarchs whose algorithms dictate our lives ("the heroes are running on empty," Serge seethes). The bridge is the sober awakening, where the elite suddenly realise: "I'm a stone-cold killer".

"We find ourselves, somehow, at the whim of people whose intentions we don't really understand," he says.

"They're playing around with culture, and we don't really know why, or where it's going to end."

He sees the results in his teenage boys.

"If you just shout, 'Get off your phone, get off your phone', no-one wants to hear that.

"But you can subtly educate them that spending 10 hours on [the screen] is not going to do you any favours.

"Then they sit at a bus stop and, rather than get the phone out, they go, 'You know what? I'm just going to sit in these thoughts for a minute'.

"I definitely wouldn't have got to where I am now, without moments where I was just alone, thinking, 'How do I get out of this place? I want more'."

"For it to write your songs for you, I just personally find that that's taking away the bit that I like doing. Like, why would I?"

The mistake, he thinks, is that AI companies have equated writing with tedium. For Serge the studio is a playground.

"What I've learned is that the tiny little sparks are really important.

"You don't have to be too grandiose, like, 'We need a big song we can play for the rest of our lives'.

"You just think, 'That synth in the corner looks fun. I'm gonna plug it in, mess around for 10 minutes, and see what happens.'"

Eager to demonstrate, he hooks up his newest toy (a tiny desktop synth called the Moog DFAM) and tweaks its copious knobs and dials.

"I can't read instruction manuals, but I've watched YouTube tutorials," he says, generating a growling bass line that sounds like the dawning of the apocalypse.

To capture those moments of inspiration, everything in the studio is automatically recorded.

But Kasabian are selective about the music that gets released. Act III is a compact 10 songs. The guiding principle was that each one should be good enough for the setlist.

They've been previewing the album all summer, from Japan to Turkey. And in June, they delivered the biggest headline show of their career, in London's Finsbury Park.

It's a remarkable turn of events. Just six years ago, Kasabian sacked singer Tom Meighan , one day before he was convicted of assaulting his partner .

"The pain was unbearable," says Serge, "But we couldn't let the story end there.

"This is my life's work, in a way, so we had to give it a go."

Serge stepped up as frontman and, to his surprise, Kasabian gained a new lease of life.

Today, their shows are more theatrical and more communal, shedding (some of) the beer-soaked rowdiness of their first incarnation.

Commercially, they're at the top of their game, too. If Act III tops the charts next week, Kasabian will beat Led Zeppelin's tally of having seven consecutive studio albums go to number one.

"That's why Finsbury Park meant so much, because we never thought we'd have days like that again," says Serge.

Becoming the frontman has "changed my life completely", he adds.

Instead of drinking to prepare for a show, he runs (inspired by his wife, who is just 46 seconds shy of a championship place at the London Marathon).

"It's been a seismic shift in my whole being.

"I want people to leave these shows with memories that are laser-beamed into their brains for the rest of their lives. So it's a commitment to that attitude, and getting fit's been a major part of it."

It's hard to imagine this man, quietly sipping a cup of tea in his slippers, commanding crowds of thousands.

"If you saw the kid I was at school, you wouldn't be like, 'Okay, that's definitely someone that's gonna be a singer'.

"But I have no real control once I get on stage. It turns out my natural disposition is pure energy, because I just feel the music."

So, is it true he'll bring that energy to Oasis's rumoured Knebworth shows next summer?

"I've not heard that rumour," he says. "But who wouldn't do it if they were asked?"

Whatever happens, Kasabian are on an upward trajectory.

There are even plans for a 10th album taking shape on a whiteboard in the corner of the studio.

"You're naughty!" he says when I mention it. "That's what I get for having a journo looking about the studio.

"But yes, that's exactly right. The fishing rod is out, and I'm looking for a big fish."

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln to dock at Thailand's Pattaya resort after 250 days at sea
articles.summary: The ship is docking close to Pattaya, known for its raucous nightlife, and for sex tourism.
articles.body:
After a record 250 days at sea without a port stop, the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln is preparing to dock in Thailand, giving its nearly 5,000 crew members a much-needed break.

The ship is docking close to the beach resort of Pattaya, known for its raucous nightlife and for sex tourism. For the US it also carries strong historical echoes.

When the weary sailors walk into the city's bars and restaurants, they will literally be treading in the footsteps of the hundreds of thousands of US troops who came here for R&R – rest and relaxation - during the Vietnam War.

They transformed it from a sleepy fishing village to one of the world's most famous and frenetic party towns.

Today the neon-lit alleys running down to the beach are much quieter than usual. The bars in the city's famous Walking Street still screen videos on their walls of pole-dancing women, trying to lure customers inside.

But there are not many of those customers, and most seem to be family groups from the Middle East more interested in the Turkish ice-cream vendor than the go-go bars.

The Iran War, which has affected tourism and consumer spending, has hit businesses hard here. The prospect of thousands of American sailors, with nine months of salary unspent while at sea, offers a rare opportunity to local businesses.

The US carrier left San Diego last November on what was supposed to be a six-month assignment in the Pacific and South China Sea.

However, the ship was diverted to the Gulf after the US and Israel began military operations against Iran in late February.

Recently some members of Congress raised concern about reports of food shortages, broken toilets and mental stress among the crew. The US Navy acknowledged that working conditions have been tough, but said the crew were sufficiently well-supported. It would not, however, comment to the BBC on the carrier docking at Pattaya, citing operational security.

Despite its close relationship with China, Thailand is a treaty ally of the US, and port visits by US Navy ships are a familiar occurrence.

But this is probably the largest number of US military personnel coming straight from a war zone to Pattaya since the fall of Saigon in 1975.

"This visit could be our best hope," said Anon Saiteer, who sells gems in a shop near Walking Street, which has put up a large sign welcoming the US sailors and marines and offering them a special discount. "We have nothing to lose – we just hope they will spend some money here."

But US and Thai officials are trying to ensure this happens without any of the salacious headlines for which Pattaya has become known.

The Thai authorities have said there are a few places where the US servicemen and women will not be allowed to go. One of them is Soi 6 which runs down to the main beach, and is known for its concentration of racy go-go bars.

While the Thai police have reminded their US visitors that prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand, there are actually thought to be 25,000 to 50,000 sex workers in the city. Many of them work in Soi 6, where they stand outside the bars imploring men to come inside.

The many cannabis shops in Pattaya are also off-limits to US crew members, along with sea-sports like paragliding and jet-skis.

"It is their decision," Mayor Poramase Ngampiches told the BBC. "The US military have done their homework."

The US Navy has organised shuttle buses from the port into Pattaya running from 5am to 2am every day the carrier is here in Thailand. Two hotels have been designated suitable for those US crew members who want to splash out on a night onshore.

The Thai authorities have deployed hundreds of police officers to keep an eye on the city's entertainment zones, and warned local businesses not to overcharge their American guests.

"The visits of US military men 50-60 years ago introduced Pattaya to the world and turned it into a tourist attraction," says Mayor Poramase. "We have to be frank, the city has a reputation for bar girls. We understand the stereotypes. We can't stop that. What we can do is to show that Pattaya has changed, that we now have other things, such as sports, seminars, wellness and family-friendly activities. It's a mixture of everything."

Both countries hope that by the time the USS Abraham Lincoln begins the long journey home across the Pacific on 6 September, it will be with a refreshed and rested crew.

articles.title: Tiger Woods to change plea after DUI crash arrest in Florida
articles.summary: The golfer will be in court on Wednesday for a hearing to change his plea after being charged with driving under the influence.
articles.body:
Tiger Woods has been scheduled to appear in court for a hearing to change his plea five months after a rollover crash in Florida led to him being charged with driving under the influence.

Court records show the hearing is set for Wednesday in Martin County, Florida. The golfer was arrested after the March crash, and had passed a breathalyser test but declined further testing for other drugs.

He pleaded not guilty the same month to misdemeanor charges of driving under the influence and refusal to submit to testing. Woods, 50, said he was seeking treatment after the incident.

It was not immediately clear what the change of plea would be. The BBC has contacted prosecutors and Woods' attorney.

No one was injured in the crash, though Woods had to crawl out through the passenger door to free himself.

Police released body camera footage in April that captured the aftermath of the incident, showing the golfing legend after his vehicle clipped a truck and rolled over.

In the video, Woods appears calm, kneeling on one knee as he tells officers: "I looked down at my phone, and all of a sudden, boom".

He passed a breathalyser test but declined to take a urinalysis screening for other drugs, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the time.

Woods told officers he had not consumed alcohol that day. When asked about any prescription medication, he responded, "I take a few", adding he had done so earlier that morning.

He then listed the medication, though that portion of the footage was redacted.

Officers told Woods they suspected his "normal faculties" were impaired by an "unknown substance".

Authorities later reported finding two white pills in his pocket, identified as hydrocodone, an opioid commonly prescribed to treat pain.

Woods wrote on social media following the incident, "I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in today.

"I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritise my wellbeing and work toward lasting recovery."

The incident marked Woods' second arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence.
